div.head: SUBSECT. 11.
Concupiscible Appetite, as Desires, Ambition, Causes.
div.p: These Concupiscible and Irascible Appetites are as the two twists of a rope, mutually mixed one with the other, and both twining about the Heart: both good, as Austin holds, lib. 14 cap. 9 de civ. Dei: if they be moderate: both pernicious if they be exorbitant. This Concupiscible appetite, howsoever it may seem to carry with it a show of pleasure and delight, and our concupiscences most part affect us with content and a pleasing object, yet if they be in extremes, they rack and wring us on the other side. A true saying it is, Desire hath no rest: is infinite in itself, endless: and as Tho. Buoni Prob. 81.one calls it, a perpetual rack, or horse-mill, according to Austin, still going round as in a ring. They are not so continual, as diverse, facilius atomos denumerare possem, saith Tract. de Inter. do. cap. 62.Bernard, quam motus cordis; nunc haec, nunc illa cogito [I could more easily count atoms … than motions of the heart; sometimes I ponder these, sometimes those], you may as well reckon up the motes in the Sun, as them. Tract. 15 cap. 17.It extends itself to everything, as Guainerius will have it, that is superfluously sought after: or to any fervent desire, as Fernelius interprets it; be it in what kind soever, it tortures if immoderate, and is (according to 3 de alien. ment.Plater and others) an especial cause of Melancholy. Multuosis concupiscentiis dilaniantur cogitationes meae, Conf. lib. 11 cap. 29.Austin confessed, that he was torn a-pieces with his manifold desires: and so doth Bernard complain, that he could not rest for them a minute of an hour: this I would have, and that, and then I desire to be such and such. ’Tis a hard matter therefore to confine them, being they are so various and many, unpossible to apprehend all. I will only insist upon some few of the chief, and most noxious in their kind, as that exorbitant Appetite and Desire of Honour, which we commonly call Ambition: Love of money which is Covetousness, and that greedy desire of gain: self-love, pride, and inordinate desire of Vainglory or applause, Love of study in excess: Love of women (which will require a just volume of itself), of the other I will briefly speak, and in their order.

Ambition, a proud covetousness, or a dry thirst of Honour, a great torture of the mind, composed of envy, pride, and covetousness, a gallant madness,
one Hall.defines it, a pleasant poison, Ambros. lib. 3 super Lucam.Ambrose, a canker of the soul, an hidden plague: Nihil animum cruciat, nihil molestius inquietat, secretum virus, pestis occulta, &c. [Nothing so tortures the mind, nothing disturbs it more grievously, a secret venom, a hidden plague, etc.], epist. 126.Bernard, a secret poison, the father of livor, and mother of hypocrisy, the moth of holiness, and cause of madness, crucifying and disquieting all that it takes hold of. Ep. 88.Seneca calls it, rem solicitam, timidam, vanam, ventosam, a windy thing, a vain, solicitous, and fearful thing. For commonly they that like Sisyphus, roll this restless stone of Ambition, are in a perpetual Nihil infelicius his, quantus iis timor, quanta dubitatio, quantus conatus, quanta sollicitudo, nulla illis a molestiis vacua hora [Nothing is unhappier than these people, so great is their fear, so great their doubt, so great their struggle, so great their anxiety; for them no hour is free of troubles].agony, still Semper attonitus, semper pavidus, quid dicat, faciatve: ne displiceat humilitatem simulat, honestatem mentitur [Always terrified, always trembling about what he is to say or do; in order not to displease he feigns humility and pretends virtue].perplexed, semper taciti, tristesque recedunt [they always withdraw, silent and sad] (Lucretius), doubtful, timorous, suspicious, loath to offend in word or deed, still cogging and colloguing, embracing, capping, cringing, applauding, flattering, fleering, visiting, waiting at men’s doors, with all affability, counterfeit honesty and humility. If that will not serve, if once this humour (as Cypr. prolog. ad ser. To. 2. Cunctos honorat, universis inclinat, subsequitur, obsequitur, frequentat curias, visitat optimates, amplexatur, applaudit, adulatur: per fas & nefas e latebris, in omnem gradum ubi aditus patet, se ingerit, discurrit [He honours everyone, he bows down to all men, he follows, he grovels, he frequents royal courts, he visits nobles, he embraces, he applauds, he flatters; by fair means and foul he rushes out of his hiding-place, into every position as soon as it is open to an approach, he runs around].Cyprian describes it) possess his thirsty soul, ambitionis salsugo ubi bibulam animam possidet [where the saltiness of ambition seizes the parched soul], by hook and by crook he will obtain it, and from his hole he will climb to all honours and offices, if it be possible for him to get up, flattering one, bribing another, he will leave no means unassayed to win all. Turbae cogit ambitio regem inservire, ut Homerus Agamemnonem querentem inducit [Ambition forces the king to serve the mob, as Homer shows Agamemnon complaining].It is a wonder to see how slavishly these kind of men subject themselves, when they are about a suit, to every inferior person; what pains they will take, run, ride, cast, plot, countermine, protest and swear, vow, promise, what labours undergo, early up, down late; how obsequious and affable they are, how popular and courteous, how they grin and fleer upon every man they meet; with what feasting and inviting, how they spend themselves and their fortunes, in seeking that many times, which they had much better be without; as Plutarchus. Quin convivemur, & in otio nos oblectemus, quoniam in promptu id nobis fit, &c. [Why do we feast, and amuse ourselves in leisure, seeing that it is at hand for us? etc.]Cineas the Orator told Pyrrhus: with what waking nights, painful hours, anxious thoughts, and bitterness of
mind, inter spemque metumque [between hope and fear], distracted and tired, they consume the interim of their time. There can be no greater plague for the present. If they do obtain their suit, which with such cost and solicitude they have sought, they are not so freed, their anxiety is anew to begin, for they are never satisfied, nihil aliud nisi imperium spirant [they breathe nothing but power], their thoughts, actions, endeavours are all for Sovereignty and Honour, like Jovius hist. 1 lib.Lewis Sforza that huffing Duke of Milan, a man of singular wisdom, but profound ambition, born to his own, and to the destruction of Italy, though it be to their own ruin, and friends’ undoing, they will contend, they may not cease, Ut hedera arbori adhaeret, sic ambitio, &c. [As ivy cleaves to a tree, so ambition, etc.]but as a dog in a wheel, a bird in a cage, or a squirrel in a chain, so Lib. 3 de contemptu rerum fortuitarum.Budaeus compares them; they climb and climb still, with much labour, but never make an end, never at the top. A Knight would be a Baronet, and then a Lord, and then a Viscount, and then an Earl, &c., a Doctor, a Dean, and then a Bishop: from Tribune to Praetor: from Bailiff, to Mayor: first this office, and then that; as Pyrrhus in Vita Pyrrhi.Plutarch, they will first have Greece, then Africk, and then Asia, and swell with Aesop’s frog so long, till in the end they burst, or come down with Sejanus, ad Gemonias scalas [on the Gemonian steps], and break their own necks: or as Evangelus the piper in Lucian, that blew his pipe so long, till he fell down dead. If he chance to miss, and have a canvas, he is in a hell on the other side; so dejected, that he is ready to hang himself, turn Heretic, Turk, or Traitor in an instance. Enraged against his enemies, he Ambitio in insaniam facile delabitur, si excedat [Ambition readily descends into madness, if it becomes excessive]. Patritius lib. 4 tit. 20 de regis instit.rails, swears, fights, slanders, detracts, envies, murders: and for his own part, si appetitum explere non potest, furore corripitur; if he cannot satisfy his desire (as Lib. 5 de rep. cap. 1.Bodin writes) he runs mad. So that both ways, hit or miss, he is distracted so long as his Ambition lasts, he can look for no other but anxiety and care, discontent and grief in the meantime, Imprimis vero appetitus, seu concupiscentia nimia rei alicujus, honestae vel inhonestae, phantasiam laedunt, unde multi ambitiosi, Philauti, irati, avari, insani, &c. [Especially, indeed, when the desire or excessive concupiscence for something, whether honest or dishonest, damages the fantasy; whence {there are} many ambitious men, self-lovers, angry, greedy, insane, etc.] Felix Plater lib. 3 de mentis alien.madness itself, or violent death in the end. The event of this is common to be seen in populous Cities, or in Princes’ Courts, for a Courtier’s life (as Budaeus describes it) is a Budaeus de asse lib. 5.Gallimaufry of ambition, lust, fraud, imposture, dissimulation, detraction, envy, pride; the Court, a common conventicle of flatterers, time-servers, politicians, &c., or as In his Aphor.Anthony Perez will, the suburbs of hell itself. If you will see such discontented persons, there you shall likely find them. Plautus Curcul. Act. 4 Sce. 1.And which he observed of the markets of old Rome,

l.hi: Qui perjurum convenire vult hominem, mitto in Comitium;
Qui mendacem & gloriosum, apud Cluasinae sacrum;

lg.l: Dites, damnosos maritos, sub basilica quaerito, &c.
[Whoever wants to meet a perjurer, I send him to the assembly place;
Whoever a liar and braggart, to the shrine of Cloacina;
For rich and spendthrift husbands, look below the basilica, etc.]

div.p: Perjured knaves, Knights of the Post, liars, crackers, bad husbands, &c., keep their several stations; they do so still, and always did, in every commonwealth.
